name: Kogal style

card.summary: A 1990s Japanese schoolgirl fashion of micro-skirts, loose socks, platform shoes, bleached or brown hair, tan skin and bold makeup that people reference for gyaru-style hair, makeup and styling.
card.note: A fashion subculture rather than a treatment; its history includes media controversy about schoolgirls and compensated dating, which later analysis described as an overstated stereotype.

quick.overview:
Kogal (kogyaru) is a contraction of kokosei gyaru, meaning high school gal. It names Japanese high school girls who altered their uniforms with short skirts, loose socks and platform shoes, and paired them with bleached or dyed hair, tanned skin, heavy makeup and brand-name accessories. It emerged in Shibuya and Harajuku in the 1980s and peaked in the late 1990s.

For appearance, it is a reference look in gyaru styling: lightened hair, defined eyes and lips, a tan and a styled uniform or street outfit. It evolved into ganguro and yamanba and later gyaru styles such as hime gyaru, and its history is documented in encyclopedias and cultural scholarship rather than clinical research.
quick.how: Adopters describe layering a short pleated skirt, oversized slouchy socks, a loose tie or cardigan, platform shoes, lightened hair and bolder eye and lip makeup. Modern versions are worn as costume or fashion styling and mixed with other gyaru substyles.
quick.risks: No health risks are specific to the fashion. Associated practices in the 1990s, such as tanning beds and hair bleaching, carry their own skin and hair risks. School dress codes in Japan restricted uniform alterations.

lead: Kogal, or kogyaru, refers to high school-aged members of the Japanese gyaru subculture who wear their school uniforms in a distinctive style. The word contracts kokosei gyaru, high school gal, and was reportedly first used as a code by disco bouncers to spot minors [1][2].

The look combines micro-skirts, loose socks, platform shoes or boots, bleached or brown-dyed hair, artificial tans, heavy makeup and accessories such as Burberry-check scarves and decorated phones. Girls favoured Shibuya's 109 building and Harajuku [1].

Its relevance to someone changing how they look is as a reference style for gyaru-influenced hair, makeup and outfit styling. It is documented through fashion history and media studies rather than clinical research [1][2].

chain: Altered uniform, hair colour and bold makeup
angle.text: Adopters copy the layered, high-contrast styling, lighter hair and defined makeup of the look. It functions as a fashion template rather than a physical-change method.

paras: Kogals modified standard school uniforms to defy dress codes: shortened skirts, oversized loose socks bunched at the ankles and held with glue or tape, and platform shoes [1][2]. Hair was bleached or dyed brown, skin darkened with tanning, and makeup heavier than school rules allowed [1][2]. Photo booths and designer or imitation brand goods were common elements [1].

Wikipedia dates the first kogals to the 1980s, when middle-school dropouts from private schools shortened their skirts where the yankii subculture lengthened theirs; teen gyaru magazines appeared in the 1970s, with Popteen running monthly since 1980 [1]. A 1993 TV special, Za Kogyaru Naito, brought the look to a mass audience [1][2]. Singer Namie Amuro popularised platform shoes in 1994, Egg magazine launched in 1995, and kogal culture peaked in 1998 [1].
Grokipedia connects the style to Japan's bubble economy, rising teen spending power and loosening uniform rules, though it is an AI-generated source [2].

In the mid-1990s ganguro, with dark tanning and heavier makeup, promoted through Egg, displaced the original look, followed by the more extreme yamanba [1]. After the late 1990s kogal faded from media attention, while gyaru styles such as shiro gyaru, onee gyaru and the princess-style hime gyaru (from 2007) emerged [1].

Critics accused kogals of conspicuous consumption, and some were linked in media to enjo kosai, compensated dating, which was sensationalised in the mid-1990s and in the 1997 film Bounce Ko Gals. Later analysis treated the panic as an overstated stereotype, and some scholars said coverage fetishised school uniforms and blamed the girls who wore them, while others saw kogals as asserting independence [1][2].
